rows.title: Introduction to Asian American and Pacific Islander Studies
rows.heading: Upon successful completion of the course the student will be able to
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course the student will be able to:
outcomes: Upon successful completion of the course the student will be able to:
Evaluate the impact of student and community activism on the creation of Ethnic Studies and Asian American studies.

Analyze and articulate common Ethnic Studies concepts and terms such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethno-centrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, and anti-racism in analyzing the experiences of Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders.

Apply theory and knowledge produced by AAPI communities to describe the histories, critical events, contributions, intellectual traditions, lived-experiences, and social struggles of Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders in the United States, emphasizing agency and group-affirmation.

Identify shared experiences that link Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders together, as well as the internal diversity (class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, tribal citizenship, sovereignty, language, and/or age) that characterizes this diverse group.

Use the lens of anti-colonialism, anti-racism, and equity for Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders to critically analyze how (settler) colonialism, imperialism, militarism, and racial capitalism shape AAPI historical and contemporary experiences particularly their (im)migration and/or displacement and their social and political exclusion in the US.

Evaluate the impacts of federal, state, and local laws in relation to Asian immigrants, Asian Americans, and Pacific Islanders on Asian American and Pacific Islander communities, particularly with respect to family formation, ethnic community development, and identity.

Critically analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, national origin, immigration status, sovereignty, language, and/or age in Asian American and Pacific Islander communities.

Critically review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced, enacted, and studied by Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders are relevant to current and structural issues such as anti-immigrant sentiment, anti-Asian violence, U.S. military industrial complex, environmental racism, and settler-colonialism.

Critically examine primary and/or secondary sources created by Asian American and Pacific Islander cultural producers–memoir, fiction, major motion picture, documentary, oral history(ies) and other lived experiences, or other art forms–to clarify how Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders challenge negative stereotypes and resist social and political marginalization in the US.

Describe and actively engage with anti-racist and anti-colonial issues, the practices and movements in AAPI communities, as well as other racial and ethnic coalitional groups for a just and equitable society.
The following topics are included in the framework of the course but are not intended as limits on content. The order of presentation and relative emphasis will vary with each instructor.
Introduction to Asian American and Pacific Islander Studies
Who are Asian Americans? Who are Pacific Islanders?
Census data and the emergence of Asian Pacific American label
Issues with Asian Pacific American label
The political power of pan-ethnic identities such as AAPI, Asian American and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (AANHPI), and  Asian Pacific Islander Desi American (APIDA) labels
Why Asian American and Pacific Islander Studies?
Defining Ethnic Studies: Foundations, Concepts, and Theories
Critical Race Theory: race, ethnicity, racism, racialization
Imperialism, settler colonialism, racial/ global capitalism, neocolonialism, and militarism
The racial triangulation of Asian Americans theory
Western Imperialism, US Capitalism and Asian Migration to the US
Western imperialism and push factors in Asian countries
Capitalism and pull factors in the United States
The US empire in the Philippines
The US empire in American Samoa
US military colonialism in Chamorro and Guam
Asian Exclusion, Citizenship and the Law
Legal and political surveillance of Asian bodies in 19th century California
California Foreign Miners’ Tax of 1850 and 1852
“An Act to Discourage the Immigration to this State of Persons Who Cannot Become Citizens Thereof” state law (1855)
California State Constitution of 1879 Anti-Chinese provisions
United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind (1923)
US nationals – neither aliens nor citizens
Japanese internment, race, and cultural citizenship
Hawaiian blood quantum and the politics of race, citizenship, and entitlement
US Militarism, Wars, Movements and Memories
Racist Violence and the Formation of Ethnic Enclave
US settler colonialism, racial capitalism, and Anti-Asian violence
The formation of Asian American ethnic enclaves
Anti-war movement and Asian American coalition
Third World Liberation Front (1968) and the origins of Ethnic Studies and Asian American Studies
Black Power movement, Yellow Power movement, and the Asian American Political Alliance (1968)
Selected Contemporary Issues Facing AAPI Communities (discussed in comparison with issues facing other communities of color in the US)
The underrepresentation/ misrepresentation of Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders in American popular culture
Education and the Model Minority Myth
Anti-Muslim and anti-immigrant sentiment and policies
Gentrification and the racial commodification of Asian American ethnic enclaves
Racial triangulation of Asian Americans, wedge politics, and inter-racial relations
Globalization, racial capitalism, and labor exploitation
The Intersectionality of Race, Class, Gender, Sexuality, Nationality and Citizenship, and AAPI Experience
Sexuality, anti-Asian immigration laws, and queer AAPI Experience
The social and political marginalization of H-4 visa holders (spouses of highly skilled Asian temporary workers – the H-1B visa holders)
Introduction to Asian Americans’ & Pacific Islanders’ arts and literature
Asian Americans’ and Pacific Islanders’ involvement in media production
AAPI Social Movements, Community Activism, and Politics
The Pacific indigenous rights & sovereignty movements
The International Hotel struggle, San Francisco
Black Lives Matter and inter-racial coalition building
Political imagination & future directions in Asian American and Pafic Islander Studies and "Asian Pacific America"
Reading assignments are required and may include, but are not limited to, the following:
Assigned textbooks focused on Asian American and Pacific Islander studies.
Primary and secondary sources including document collections, novels/fiction, memoirs/autobiographies, major motion pictures, documentaries, and oral histories.

Articles from scholarly journals such as: A. Amerasia Journal; B.Contemporary Pacific: A Journal of Island Affairs; C. Hulili: Multidisciplinary Research on Hawaiian Well-Being; D. Journal of Asian American Studies; E. MANOA: A Pacific Journal of International Writing; and, F.Journal of Southeast Asian American Education & Advancement (JSAAEA).

Articles from Asian American periodicals/magazines such as: A. Asian American Policy Review; B. Asian American Law Journal; C. Asian Pacific American Law Journal; D. AAPI nexus: Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders, Policy Practice and Community; and E. Hyphen: Asian America Unabridged.
Reports from AAPI serving organizations and institutions such as Stop AAPI Hate and Asian Americans Advancing Justice.
Writing assignments are required and may include, but are not limited to, the following:

Expository essays critically analyzing how settler colonialism, imperialism, racial capitalism, globalization, war, American empire, citizenship, and various aspects of identity such as race, class, gender, and sexuality have shaped AAPI experiences and their social justice movements.
Brief descriptions and analyses of persons, places, institutions, and events of historical significance to Asian American and Pacific Islander studies.
Analytical reviews of a book, major motion picture, or novel dealing with the contemporary AAPI experience.

Research papers/argumentative essays on a specific topic in the AAPI experience, or an AAPI-related topic covered during the semester. Biographical essays synthesizing primary sources, secondary sources, and oral history focused on the AAPI experience.
Newspaper/ Magazines articles and op-eds about current issues facing AAPI communities
Outside assignments may include, but are not limited to, the following:
Read, take notes, and study the assigned texts.
Prepare for objective exams, in-class essays, and class discussions related to the AAPI experience.
Research and prepare for in-class and on-line multimedia presentations.
Complete take-home essays and papers that critically analyze topics in AAPI studies.
Conduct oral history interview(s) to document and contextualize the lived experiences of AAPI community members.
Participate in / Conduct community-based participatory research
Create and maintain a blog, a newsletter, a student newspaper covering AAPI – related school/ community activities, events, and issues.
Organize AAPI – related panel discussions/ workshops/ events

Engage in community service-learning activities organized by the instructor and local AAPI-serving organizations to understand more about issues impacting AAPI communities and AAPI community activism.
Appropriate Assignments that Demonstrate Critical Thinking:
Critical thinking assignments are required and may include, but are not limited to, the following:

Expository essays comparing and contrasting the experiences of different indigenous Pacific Islanders of the Hawaiian Islands, Guam (Chamorro), and/or American Samoa in at least two of the following topics: settler colonialism, resistance, self-determination, U.S. imperialism, the U.S. military industrial complex, and citizenship.
In-person or on-line multi-media presentations describing and analyzing the impact of immigration policies and anti-Asian laws on Asian American communities.

Analyze primary sources documenting anti-Asian sentiment, violence, and rhetoric, including newspaper articles, images in pop culture magazines and other media, and political speeches, and write anti-racism op-ed articles.
Research papers and argumentative essays analyzing the long-term and short-term impacts of the U.S. militarism and militourism on Pacific Islands

Critical reflective essays evaluating Asian American and Pacific Islander engagement with their own intersectional identities, including generational differences, and the development of Hapa (mixed-race) and biracial/multiracial second-generation AAPI.

Critical autobiography detailing how the student’s life intersects wih AAPI history and/or how different forces shaping the experiences of Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders (such as US colonialism, imperialism, militarism, capitalism, and racism) might have also shaped student life and experience.
A student's grade will be based on multiple measures of performance unless the course requires no grade. Multiple measures may include, but are not limited to, the following:

Other: Quizzes and objective exams In-class essay examinations Take-home essay examinations Writing assignments Research projects Book reviews Class participation Participation in community service-learning activities

Formulate functions that capture key abstractions, prevent duplication of code or data, and transform parameters and return values.

Use logical constructs and recursion to operate upon data structures.
Explain how a programming language can be extended to create a vocabulary that is proximal to the problem domain.

Systematically design and implement introductory-level programs from given specifications, such as problem descriptions, user stories, design criteria, input/output scenarios, functional or unit tests, pseudo code, modeling language specifications or diagrams.

Articulate the purpose and working of introductory-level programs, and their language constructs and data structures, such as through diagrams (for instance, flowcharts, Unified Modelling Language (UML) diagrams or entity-relationship (ER) diagrams), code comments, screencast videos, interactive computing notebooks (for instance, Jupyter notebooks), or other written or oral communication.

Document external interfaces of introductory-level functions or methods (the application programming interface (API)), and the inner working of introductory-level functions, or methods in-code comments.

Systematically test and debug introductory-level programs by interactively entering arguments, utilizing functional or unit tests, running programs in a test environment, or using a debug environment (for instance, a debugger in an integrated development environment (IDE)).
Develop introductory-level programs using industry recognized tools, such as code editors, command lines (Read, execute, print loop, REPL), emulators, or integrated development environments (IDE).
Create a fully functional, interactive introductory-level program incorporating a substantial set of topics from the course.

Express a problem as a set of logic clauses in the programming language Prolog and use them to solve a problem.

rows.heading: Upon successful completion of the course the student will be able to
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course the student will be able to:
outcomes: Upon successful completion of the course the student will be able to:
Select and use cameras and lenses to successfully expose black and white film and develop images.
Distinguish and demonstrate the basic techniques of camera operation through manual exposure, lens focusing, metering methods, and film loading.
Select and prepare darkroom chemicals, implement film processing techniques, and use film processing equipment to produce black and white photographs.
Apply the principles of light theory to create black and white photographs.
Analyze and employ visualization and compositional techniques to produce black and white darkroom images.
Demonstrate the use of silver gelatin paper and print finishing techniques to create black and white photographs.
Recognize and interpret photography as an art form through the analysis of diverse historical and contemporary black and white photographs.
The following topics are included in the framework of the course but are not intended as limits on content. The order of presentation and relative emphasis will vary with each instructor.
Creation of original black and white images

rows.title: Electric Lineman IA
rows.heading: Upon successful completion of the course the student will be able to
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course the student will be able to:
outcomes: Upon successful completion of the course the student will be able to:
Demonstrate ability to manipulate mathematical computation using fractions, decimals, percent, algebra, and fundamentals of trigonometry.
Demonstrate the knowledge in using fundamental mechanics: weight, pressure, torque, power, and vectors.
Demonstrate the knowledge of electron theory as it applies to conductors, electrical potential, current, impedance, and simple circuits.
Demonstrate the knowledge in applying the fundamentals of magnetism as it pertains to permanent and electromagnets, magnetic flux, and reluctance.
The following topics are included in the framework of the course but are not intended as limits on content. The order of presentation and relative emphasis will vary with each instructor.
Reading assignments are required and may include, but are not limited to, the following:
Power delivery industry articles from internet sites, such as www.lineworker.com and www.tdworld.com.
Writing assignments are required and may include, but are not limited to, the following:
Summarize the electron theory and the molecular structure of matter.
Written short essays on fundamental mechanics.
Outside assignments may include, but are not limited to, the following:
Research web sites, such as www.lineworker.com and linmenonline.com.
Prepare research reports on the magnetic circuit.
Appropriate Assignments that Demonstrate Critical Thinking:
Critical thinking assignments are required and may include, but are not limited to, the following:
Analyze Ohm's Law and how it relates to the electron theory.
Compare and contrast permanent magnets and electromagnets.
Identify and describe the molecular structure of matter, explaining ionization.
Analyze how weight, pressure, and force affect work output and energy.
A student's grade will be based on multiple measures of performance unless the course requires no grade. Multiple measures may include, but are not limited to, the following:
Other: Written or oral examinations Outside assignments including writing assignments Class discussion Class participation Attendance per current apprenticeship policies
